Name: cloud_regime_attribution_albedo_2023
Title: Cloud Regime Fingerprints of the 2023 Albedo Decline: A Machine-Learning Attribution Approach
Experiment: 1) Datasets: CERES-EBAF Ed4.1 top-of-atmosphere radiative fluxes and cloud fractions, ERA5 hourly reanalysis for meteorological predictors (subsidence, lower-tropospheric stability, SST, free-tropospheric humidity, surface winds), MODIS Collection 6.1 aerosol optical depth, ISCCP-H cloud-type classifications, and CMIP6 DAMIP and CESM2-LE (40-member) single-forcing simulations. 2) Metrics: global planetary albedo, net absorbed shortwave radiation anomaly, low-cloud fraction, and regional cloud radiative effect contributions (W m⁻²). Attribution is quantified via the fractional contribution of aerosol forcing, internal variability, and feedback to the 2023 albedo drop, with uncertainty ranges from bootstrapping across ensemble members. 3) Baseline comparisons: (a) standard multiple linear regression of albedo on aerosol optical depth and Niño3.4 index; (b) a simple energy balance model forced with CERES fluxes; (c) direct CMIP6 multi-model mean attribution without downscaling. 4) Expected outcomes: The emulator-based decomposition will attribute ~35–50% of the low-cloud decline to sulfate aerosol reductions from shipping and industry, ~20–30% to a persistent shift in subtropical cloud regimes (potentially an emerging feedback), and the remainder to transient internal variability associated with La Niña–El Niño transition. We expect the new method to reduce uncertainty by at least 30% relative to linear regression. 5) Ablation studies: (a) removing the cloud regime segmentation and using global mean quantities only; (b) replacing the CNN emulator with a random forest to test nonlinearity sensitivity; (c) omitting the ship-track masking and using only hemispheric aerosol indices; (d) training the emulator on fewer ensemble members (e.g., 10) to assess generalization error. These will isolate the added value of fine-scale regime separation and the neural network's capacity to capture nonlinear aerosol–cloud interactions.
